Second, on that understanding nobody ever completes faith; and one cannot add to something that has not yet been completed.

Reply: This applies only to those who hold that faith disappears whenever any required work or abstention is absent, as among the Muʿtazilites and Khārijites. It does not apply to those who hold that faith continues as long as assent remains, as is attributed to the early authorities. On the latter account, however, increase and decrease concern the perfection of faith, not its fundamental existence.

Hence al-Rāzī proposes a reconciliation: passages indicating that faith is invariable refer to its root or basis, while passages indicating variation refer to its completed form.

Yet one might reply: we do not accept that assent itself cannot vary. Assent can be stronger or weaker, as in assent to the rising of the sun compared with assent to the world's temporal origination. Either assent is itself belief (iʿtiqād), which admits of degrees, or it is grounded upon that belief and varies with it. There are also degrees in extent: general assent and detailed assent to some, more, or still more particulars. These differences count as faith, because they concern assenting to what the Prophet brought: generally concerning what is grasped generally, and in detail concerning what is grasped in detail.

Objection: The required assent must reach the degree of certainty, which does not vary; variation would imply a possibility of the contrary remaining.

Reply: Certainty (yaqīn) belongs to the category of knowledge and cognition; it has already been argued that these are not identical with assent.

Certainty has levels, from the clearest of self-evident propositions to the most obscure of theoretical conclusions. The claim that such degrees involve nothing but differences in clarity and obscurity is rejected; even after certainty is attained and hesitation has ceased, degrees remain.

Witness Abraham's request, despite his already possessing assent: “But so that my heart may become tranquil.” And the saying attributed to ʿAlī: “If the veil were lifted, I would not increase in certainty.”

title: Faith at death and the faith of the imitator
en:
...This does not remove the previously mentioned risk of a misleading implication, nor explain what specially connects religious etiquette and the quest for blessing to **faith**, rather than to the remaining acts of worship and obedience.

**Second explanation:** The assent on which **deliverance** depends is an inward, concealed matter. It is subject to numerous hidden obstacles—desire, the devil, and abandonment by divine aid. Although a person may be certain that he possesses faith, he cannot be sure that something incompatible with final salvation does not secretly taint it, especially when he considers the detailed, difficult commands and prohibitions opposed to natural inclination and pleasure, without being aware of that obstacle.

He therefore leaves the attainment [or integrity] of such faith to God's will. This answer would be quite plausible **were it not for its tension** with the consensus claimed by the opposing group and with the reports cited in the collections of legal opinions (*fatāwā*).

**Third explanation—the one to be relied upon:** Imām al-Ḥaramayn says that present faith is **certainly established now**, without doubt, but the faith that serves as the **sign of triumph and deliverance** is *faith at life's end* (*īmān al-muwāfāt*). It is to that faith that the early authorities particularly referred when joining their profession of belief to God's will. They did **not** intend to cast doubt upon faith presently attained.

The word *muwāfāt* means **arriving at the end of life and the beginning of the hereafter**. Faith that saves, or unbelief that destroys, is the faith or unbelief **present at that decisive moment**, even if it has been preceded by the opposite—not a state that obtained earlier and was then changed into its contrary.

Accordingly many Ashʿarites say that what counts is faith at death and the corresponding blessedness. They mean that it is what **finally saves**, not that present faith is not genuine faith or present unbelief not genuine unbelief. The same reasoning concerns blessedness and misery, friendship with God and enmity towards Him.

This answers the objection that, if a person has faith in truth, he is **truly a believer** and cannot say “I am a believer, if God wills,” any more than “I am alive, if God wills.” Indeed, whoever is truly a believer is a believer before God and in God's knowledge even if God knows that he will later change. Whoever is presently a believer is now a friend of God and blessed; whoever is presently an unbeliever is now His enemy and wretched. As a believer can become an unbeliever, so a friend can become an enemy, and a blessed person wretched—**and conversely**.

As for the sayings attributed to them that “the blessed never becomes wretched; the wretched never becomes blessed,” and “blessed is the one blessed in his mother's womb, wretched the one wretched in his mother's womb,” their meaning is this: someone whom God knows will possess **the blessedness that counts at life's end** will not pass from that final blessedness to its opposite, and likewise for wretchedness, friendship, and enmity. The relevant “blessed” person is the one God knows will **end** blessed; the corresponding claim about misery follows.

In summary, the believer does **not** doubt that faith truly exists in him now, nor is the point of the formula to replace his firm commitment to continuing in it. Rather, he **fears an evil end** and **hopes for a good conclusion**. He therefore connects the faith of life's end—the sign of salvation, victory, and attainment of spiritual degrees—to God's will.

This conforms to God's instruction, “Do not say of anything, ‘I shall do it tomorrow,’ except [adding] ‘if God wills.’” May God make our lives and deaths belong to that faith, grant us a good ending, and enable us to win the noblest provision through the Prophet and his family.

**Fifth investigation — the faith of the imitator (*īmān al-muqallid*).** Many scholars, including all the jurists as al-Taftāzānī reports, maintain that an imitator's faith is **valid** and has its corresponding consequences in this world and the next. Abū al-Ḥasan [al-Ashʿarī], the Muʿtazilites, and many speculative theologians are reported to reject it.

**Argument for validity:** The reality of faith is assent, and in the imitator assent is present, without any accompanying cause that would itself negate faith.

**Objection:** Assent cannot be conceived without knowledge, because knowledge is either **essential to it** or a **condition** of it, as discussed earlier. The imitator has no such knowledge: knowledge is a firm, correct belief founded on a **ground**, either immediate necessity or inference.

**Reply:** What counts in assent is **certainty**, that is, firm and correct conviction. It may even be sufficient that the belief conforms to reality, treating **a predominant opinion** whose contrary never occurs to the mind as equivalent to certainty.

A further reply says assent may exist **without knowledge or cognition**, and vice versa. We believe in prophets and angels without knowing them individually; we believe in all the circumstances of the Resurrection—the reckoning, Balance, Bridge, and so forth—without knowing their modes and precise characteristics. The People of the Book knew the Prophet, according to the Qurʾān, as they knew their own sons, yet they were not believers.

**Qualification:** This requires examination. What is meant is **knowledge of precisely what is assented to**. We know of the prophets and angels whatever we assent to concerning them. Hence the impossibility of assent without knowledge—understood as *conviction*—is certain. The remaining issue concerns the **converse**: knowledge without assent.

**New objection:** We need not deny that imitation produces something rightly called faith and assent. We contend instead that it **does not benefit** its possessor, just as the faith of one who believes upon seeing unavoidable punishment (*īmān al-yaʾs*) is of no avail. Abū Manṣūr al-Māturīdī reportedly explains the latter ineffectiveness by the inability then to infer **the unseen from the seen** and so ground one's profession on inferential knowledge. On this argument, reward for faith corresponds not to simply attaining the first assent but to **enduring the difficulty** of disciplined thought, sustained attention to the prophets' miracles or the world's originated things, and discrimination between proof and sophistical doubt.

**Reply:** Textual evidence establishes the ineffectiveness of the **despairing faith produced at the sight of punishment**, not the faith of the imitator. Consensus, likewise, concerns the former only.

Even if analogy (*qiyās*) were accepted as valid in such fundamental religious questions, it has not been established that the reason for the rule is the reason proposed by the opponents.

Indeed al-Māturīdī and many investigators explain the ineffectiveness of faith at the moment of unavoidable punishment otherwise: it is a **faith aimed merely at warding off punishment**, not genuine faith; and by then the person no longer possesses the freedom to dispose of and benefit from his own life. The punishment of this life is a prelude to punishment in the hereafter, since he may die under it and pass immediately to the latter. The case of imitative faith is different, for such a person's faith is a seeking to draw near...

title: Proof, imitation, and the capacities of ordinary believers
en:
...**drawing near to God** and seeking His satisfaction, without compulsion, without aiming merely to ward off punishment, and without the loss of the ability to dispose of oneself. Such faith differs in kind from profession at the instant of unavoidable punishment.

**Those who deny validity or salvific benefit to the imitator's faith** do not all make the same requirement. Some say that it is not necessary for each article of belief to depend upon a separate **rational inference**. It suffices to rely on the word of one whose prophethood has already been established by a miracle, whether witnessed personally or reliably transmitted, or on consensus. Thus a person may accept from the Prophet that the world originated, that a Maker exists, and that the Maker is one.

Others require that belief in **every foundational question** rest upon a rational proof, yet do not require the person to be able to **articulate the proof**, dispute with adversaries, or repel every objection. This is the position commonly ascribed to Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī. It has even been related from him that someone lacking it is not a believer.

ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Baghdādī nevertheless says that, even if al-Ashʿarī does not call such a person a believer **without qualification**, he does not call him an unbeliever, since assent is present. Rather he sins by neglecting inquiry and inference; God may pardon him or punish him in proportion to the neglect, but his final destination is Paradise. This suggests that al-Ashʿarī means **not a believer in the fullest sense**, much as with omissions of works. Otherwise he would either affirm the **intermediate station** or admit a nonbeliever to Paradise, neither of which is his doctrine. On this interpretation, no substantive disagreement remains.

A third group requires, in addition to proof-based assent, the ability to **debate opponents** and **resolve the objections** they raise. This is attributed to the Muʿtazilites. They do not judge a person incapable of these tasks to have faith, and Abū Hāshim is reported even to pronounce him an unbeliever.

If their claim is based on taking **neglect of inquiry** as a grave sin which expels a person from faith when it occurs later, and excludes entry into faith when present at the outset, the dispute reduces to the **earlier question of the grave sinner**. If instead they say that this kind of assent **does not suffice for faith or does not benefit**, that is another question. Their proofs suggest this latter interpretation.

**First proof of those rejecting imitation:** The reality of faith is to put oneself in security against being **falsely informed, deceived, or misled**. On this etymology, the *ifʿāl* form of *īmān* may be causative or indicate entering a state, as though the believer became secure. Such security, they maintain, can come only from knowledge.

**Reply:** In the relevant construction, the person protected is the **informant**, not the hearer: one says *āmantu bi-hi* or *lahu*, “I believed him.” The appropriate sense of derivation from *amn* is therefore **making the other secure from contradiction and accusation of lying**, as the Muʿtazilites themselves acknowledge. That occurs through assent whether or not obtained by inference. Even if security against being deceived were what is intended, it could be gained through a **firm conviction** acquired by imitation.

**Second proof:** What is obligatory is **knowledge**, and knowledge arises only through necessity or inference. It does not arise here through necessity; therefore inference is indispensable.

**Reply:** We do not dispute the **obligation to consider and infer**. The question is whether omission of that duty makes existing assent **religiously invalid**. One might even say that the purpose of proof is **to arrive at assent**; once that goal is attained, the absence of the usual means does not in itself nullify the end.

**Third proof:** The foundational doctrine imitated is either **false** or **true**. If false, imitating it is invalid by agreement, as illustrated by Jews, Christians, Magians and idol-worshippers imitating their forebears. If true, how is its truth known? If only by imitation, there is a circle; if by proof, the claim to imitate contradicts itself.

**Reply:** The question concerns doctrines **already known by proof to be true**, such as duties necessarily known to belong to Islam: does someone who assents to these through reliance on other people count as a believer, subject to the worldly and otherworldly judgements of faith, **even if he sins by neglecting theoretical investigation**? That is the actual point of dispute.

The further assertion that “itself permitting imitation” either lacks proof and is false or rests on proof and so is inconsistent is an **obvious equivocation**. Nor should one object that imitation fails to discharge the **whole obligation of obtaining knowledge** in the religious foundations: there is no dispute about that failure. These weak arguments are unnecessary to establish the **independent duty of investigation**, which the author regards as grounded in text and consensus.

It has in fact been reported of al-Kaʿbī, Ibn Abī ʿAyyāsh, and other Muʿtazilites that rational persons are not all charged with exactly the same task. Some are charged with inquiry—the people capable of investigation—while others are charged with **imitation and probable conviction**: ordinary people, slaves, and, in the social classification reported by the source, many women, because they are said to be unable to investigate and distinguish proofs from sophisms. Such people are required to imitate **someone in the right**, not one in error, and to have the **correct** predominant opinion, not the wrong one.

Some later writers in the same school say that those unable to pursue complex proof must at least hear the **first, easily understood elements of demonstration**. If they understand them, that suffices; such people are called **people of the general articles** (*aṣḥāb al-jumal*) and need not formulate polished arguments. Those unable even to grasp these elements, according to the reported view, are not legally charged with them at all; they are described as created for the worldly benefit of those who are charged. The source lists many ordinary people, slaves and women under that social judgement.

In theologians' terminology, a “person of the general articles” is one who assents to the **general propositions on which members of the religious community agree**, without entering into their contested details. He accepts whatever agrees with those general propositions and rejects whatever contradicts them.

These general propositions include: God is one, without partner or equal; He existed before time, place, Throne, and every creature; He is eternal while all else is originated; He is just in judgement and true in report; He does not love corruption or approve unbelief in His servants, nor—on the reported formulation—charge them beyond capacity; He is wise and acts well in all He does, creates, judges, and determines.

The summary continues: God sent messengers and revealed books so that those whom He knew would take heed and fear would do so, and that the proof would be completed against those He knew would refuse belief. Acceptance of His decree and submission to His command are obligatory; what He wills comes to be and what He does not will does not; He guides whom He wills and leaves astray whom He wills, but not with the sort of misleading ascribed to Satan. The last phrase continues into the following source unit.

title: Classification of unbelief and disputes among ahl al-qibla
en:
...**the absolutely greatest punishment**, it applies only to the very worst kinds of unbelief. If it means the greatest punishment **relative to a lesser one**, it applies to many acts of disobedience. If it means “greatest compared with transgression,” while transgression is defined by incurring a punishment less than unbelief's, a **circle** results. If transgression is defined as abandoning obedience by a grave sin, some grave sins are themselves unbelief and so escape the proposed contrast; restricting grave sins to those other than unbelief reintroduces the circle. In short, this definition is manifestly **defective and obscure**.

Nor does the statement that each school defines unbelief as the contrary of whatever it calls faith work consistently: it fails altogether for the view of an **intermediate station**, and is not straightforward even on the approach of the early Sunni authorities.

**Concluding taxonomy of unbelief.** *Kāfir* means someone **lacking faith**. A person who outwardly displays faith while lacking it is specially called **hypocrite** (*munāfiq*). One who becomes an unbeliever **after entering Islam** is an **apostate** (*murtadd*), since he has turned back from Islam. One who asserts two or more deities is a **polytheist** (*mushrik*), having posited a partner in deityhood. Someone who follows a superseded scriptural religion or book is specially called a **person of the Book** (*kitābī*), as with Jews and Christians.

A person who holds **time to be beginningless** and attributes events to it is called a *dahrī*; someone who does not affirm the Maker is called a *muʿaṭṭil*. Someone who outwardly acknowledges the Prophet's prophethood and practises Islam's rites while concealing beliefs unanimously judged unbelief is designated a *zindīq*. The source offers an etymology connecting the word to the *Zand*, a book associated with Mazdak under Qubādh and allegedly presented as an interpretation of the Magian book brought by Zoroaster, whom the Magians call their prophet.

**Seventh investigation — the ruling concerning people of the qibla who disagree with the truth.** The issue is not parties who deny what is necessarily known of Islam—such as the world's origination or bodily resurrection, according to this author's list. It concerns people who agree on these essentials but differ in other foundational questions—God's attributes, the creation of actions, universality of divine will, eternity of divine speech, possibility of the beatific vision, and similar questions—where the author assumes that only **one position can be true**. Is someone holding the false position an unbeliever merely on account of that belief and profession, or not?

The author excludes a person who, despite lifelong prayer and other practices of the *ahl al-qibla*, believes in the **eternity of the world**, denies **bodily resurrection**, denies divine knowledge of **particulars**, or performs another act held to entail unbelief. Such a case, he says, is not the disputed question.

For the disputed case, al-Ashʿarī and most of his companions hold that the errant theologian is **not** an unbeliever. This is suggested by al-Shāfiʿī's reported practice of accepting the testimony of people of heterodox views, except the *Khaṭṭābiyya*, because they are said to permit falsehood. The *Muntaqā* reports from Abū Ḥanīfa that he did **not** pronounce any of the people of the qibla unbelievers; most jurists are said to follow that position. Some members of the author's school, however, affirm the excommunication of doctrinal opponents.

Early Muʿtazilites are reported to have pronounced unbelievers those who affirm eternal attributes, divine creation of human acts, and the compulsionist (*mujbira*) position. Al-Jubbāʾī is quoted as saying that a compulsionist is an unbeliever, as is anyone doubting his unbelief, and anyone doubting the unbelief of the doubter, recursively. The author strongly censures others who call unbelief the assertion of additional divine attributes, possibility of divine vision, eventual exit from the Fire, divine creation and willing of evil acts, or even the bare possibility of a miracle occurring at the hand of a liar.

Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāyīnī is reported to say: “We pronounce an unbeliever one who pronounces us unbelievers; one who does not, we do not.” Al-Rāzī's chosen position is that **no one among the people of the qibla is declared an unbeliever** merely for such disputed beliefs.

Al-Rāzī reasons that if Islam's validity depended on affirming the correct answer to every one of those contested principles, the Prophet and his successors would have demanded those answers from converts, **examined their convictions**, and instructed them in the correct positions. Certainly, the author reports, they did not do so.

Al-Rāzī distinguishes these disputes from teachings **agreed to be essentials of Islam**. Some essentials, such as bodily resurrection, are sufficiently familiar from the Qurʾān to need no further explanation. Others have easily grasped reasons suitable for **people of the general articles** (*aṣḥāb al-jumal*), such as the world's origination. Extended theological debate developed chiefly to dissolve the doubts raised by opponents. By contrast, the truth in contested fundamental questions is **subtle**, requires more thought, and may confront scriptural wording that seems to support the opposing side. If being wrong about these points constituted unbelief, explicit instruction would have been indispensable.

He then replies to the various proofs by which sects excommunicate one another. Some replies rely on the claim that violating consensus does not automatically constitute unbelief, or that consensus is not established unless anthropomorphists, corporealists, Rāfiḍites and comparable groups also agree. Others distinguish between an **implication of unbelief** and what someone actually **affirms**: the fact that a doctrine entails an unacceptable proposition does not make one who never adopts that proposition an unbeliever. Still others permit even an **apparently mistaken interpretation** without declaring the interpreter an unbeliever.

Some later Muʿtazilites agree, fearing the abyss of declaring people unbelievers whose Islam seems manifest to heaven and earth, and fearing that their own leading authorities would be caught by such excommunication. Yet, al-Taftāzānī charges, some of their writings still abound in pronouncing the great figures of Islam unbelievers, and he ends with a warning that God is mighty in retribution.

Someone may challenge al-Rāzī's inference: **general assent** to everything the Prophet brought is sufficient for valid faith, even if the person has not yet contemplated all the particulars. It is necessary to make the correct detailed position explicit only **when a particular question arises for attention**, even in matters whose denial would by consensus constitute unbelief, such as the world's origination. Many believers have no understanding of the concepts “originated” and “eternal,” nor have they thought through bodily resurrection. But **once the issue is presented**, to refuse assent to what is established as a necessary teaching would, on this author's doctrine, constitute unbelief.

**Eighth investigation — consequences of faith and unbelief.** A believer's final destiny is permanence in Paradise; an unbeliever's is permanence in Hell. The hypocrite is assigned its lowest depth. A grave sinner who remains a believer will ultimately dwell in Paradise: either immediately through pardon or intercession, or after punishment corresponding to the sin. The discussion continues into the next unit.

title: Legal and otherworldly consequences; Sunni schools; end of Chapter 3
en:
...**after punishment in the Fire proportionate to his sin**. The Muʿtazilites and Khārijites dispute these outcomes, as already described. *Fisq* is departing from obedience to God by committing a **grave sin**. The definition should be restricted to someone acting **without an admissible interpretation (*taʾwīl*)**, since the author reports agreement that a rebel (*bāghī*) acting on an interpretation is not simply called *fāsiq*. Persistent commission of minor sins—many of one sort or of several kinds—is treated as equivalent to a grave sin.

To **regard a prohibited act as lawful** (*istiḥlāl*), that is, sincerely to believe it permitted, counts as unbelief whether the sin is minor or major; likewise to **treat it as insignificant** by committing it without concern as though it were among permissibles. The judgement is intended in matters established by **decisive proof**, not every disputed legal prohibition.

The doctrinal innovator (*mubtadiʿ*)—one departing from what the author calls the path of Sunna and the Community in belief—should, he argues, receive the general otherworldly ruling of a *fāsiq*, for doctrinal neglect is not less significant than neglect in works.

As to **worldly rulings**, the believer's are evident. The diverse rulings concerning hostile unbelievers (*ḥarbī*), protected non-Muslims (*dhimmī*), persons of the Book, and apostates are dealt with in positive-law treatises. The hypocrite and *zindīq* are outwardly treated under Islamic legal judgements. Grave sinners face, as applicable under the jurists' rules, fixed punishment (*ḥadd*), discretionary correction (*taʿzīr*), a command to repent, rejection of testimony, or loss of qualification for authority—on which jurists disagree. The historical author also recommends social disapproval and avoidance of doctrinal innovators, including disapproval of prayer behind them. These prescriptions are reported **as part of the source text**, not endorsed as contemporary personal advice.

**A summary of the Sunni path, as presented by al-Taftāzānī.** The world is originated; its Maker is eternal, possessing eternal attributes which, in the technical formula, are **neither simply identical with His essence nor wholly other than it**. He is one, without likeness, contrary, peer, limit, image, or boundary. He does not inhere in another; no originated accident subsists in Him. Motion, translation, ignorance, lying, and defect cannot be predicated of Him. He will be seen in the hereafter, yet is not located in spatial extension or direction.

Whatever God wills comes to be and whatever He does not will does not. He needs nothing, and no obligation is imposed upon Him. All creatures fall under His decree, determination, intention, and will; reprehensible acts among them, however, are not objects of His **approval, command, or love**. Here the source distinguishes divine willing and creating from divine approval.

Bodily resurrection and the other transmitted doctrines—punishment in the grave, reckoning, the Bridge, Balance and the rest—are true. Unbelievers, not grave sinners who retain faith, remain eternally in the Fire; pardon and intercession are real. Signs of the Hour—including the Antichrist, Gog and Magog, Jesus' descent, the rising of the sun from the west, and the creature of the earth—are also affirmed.

Adam is the first prophet and Muḥammad the last. The first caliphs are Abū Bakr, then ʿUmar, then ʿUthmān, then ʿAlī, may God be pleased with them. Their comparative excellence is commonly ranked in that order, though the text notes some hesitation over the ranking of ʿUthmān relative to ʿAlī.

**The two principal Sunni theological affiliations.** In Khurāsān, Iraq, Syria and most other regions, the group commonly known as Ashʿarites takes its name from Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī b. Ismāʿīl, whose genealogy the text traces through Abū Burda to the Companion Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī. He is said to have first differed from Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī and to have returned from that school to **the Sunna**—defined here as the path of the Prophet—and **the Community**—the path of the Companions.

In **Transoxiana**, the Māturīdīs follow Abū Manṣūr al-Māturīdī. The source supplies a line of teachers through Abū Naṣr al-ʿIyāḍ, Abū Bakr al-Jurjānī, Abū Sulaymān al-Jurjānī and Muḥammad b. al-Ḥasan al-Shaybānī. Māturīd is identified as a village of Samarqand.

title: Why imamate is discussed in theology
en: He says: Chapter Four, on the imamate. There is no dispute that investigations concerning the imamate belong more appropriately to the science of practical rulings. They come down to this: undertaking the imamate and appointing an imam possessing the specified qualifications are collective obligations. These are matters of general concern upon which religious or worldly interests depend, and without which affairs cannot be properly ordered. The Lawgiver therefore intends that they should be accomplished overall, without intending their accomplishment by every individual. It is evident that this belongs to practical rulings rather than doctrinal ones.
ar: قال: الفصل الرابع في الإمامة. لا نزاع في أن مباحث الإمامة بعلم الفروع أليق، لرجوعها إلى أن القيام بالإمامة ونصب الإمام الموصوف بالصفات المخصوصة من فروض الكفايات، وهي أمور كلية تتعلق بها مصالح دينية أو دنيوية لا ينتظم الأمر إلا بحصولها، فيقصد الشارع تحصيلها في الجملة من غير أن يقصد حصولها من كل أحد. ولا خفاء في أن ذلك من الأحكام العملية دون الاعتقادية.

title: The office and its qualifications
en: Our works of jurisprudence state that the community must have an imam who gives life to religion, establishes the Sunna, obtains redress for the wronged, exacts what is due, and assigns rights to their proper recipients. It is stipulated that he be subject to legal responsibility, Muslim, upright, free, male, qualified for independent juristic reasoning, courageous, possessed of sound judgement and competence, able to hear, see, and speak, and of Qurashī descent. If no member of Quraysh possessing the requisite qualifications can be found, a man of Kināna is to be appointed; if none can be found, a descendant of Ishmael; and if none can be found, a non-Arab. It is not stipulated that he be a Hāshimite, immune from sin and error, or superior in merit to those over whom he is appointed.
ar: وقد ذكر في كتبنا الفقهية أنه لا بد للأمة من إمام يحيي الدين ويقيم السنة وينتصف للمظلومين ويستوفي الحقوق ويضعها مواضعها. ويشترط أن يكون مكلفا، مسلما، عدلا، حرا، ذكرا، مجتهدا، شجاعا، ذا رأي وكفاية، سميعا، بصيرا، ناطقا، قريشيا. فإن لم يوجد من قريش من يستجمع الصفات المعتبرة ولي كناني، فإن لم يوجد فرجل من ولد إسماعيل، فإن لم يوجد فرجل من العجم. ولا يشترط أن يكون هاشميا ولا معصوما ولا أفضل من يولى عليهم.

title: Election, nomination, and a council
en: The imamate is constituted in several ways. The first is the pledge of allegiance given by those empowered to bind and loose: the scholars, leaders, and prominent members of the public whose attendance can be secured. Neither a specified number nor the agreement of those in every other land is stipulated. Indeed, if the power to bind and loose rests with a single person whose authority is obeyed, his pledge is sufficient. The second is the imam’s designation and nomination of a successor. His entrusting the matter to a council is equivalent to designating a successor, except that the successor has not been individually determined: the council members deliberate and agree upon one of themselves. If the imam abdicates, that is equivalent to his death, and authority passes to the designated heir.
ar: وتنعقد الإمامة بطرق: أحدها بيعة أهل الحل والعقد من العلماء والرؤساء ووجوه الناس الذين يتيسر حضورهم، من غير اشتراط عدد ولا اتفاق من في سائر البلاد، بل لو تعلق الحل والعقد بواحد مطاع كفت بيعته. والثاني استخلاف الإمام وعهده، وجعله الأمر شورى بمنزلة الاستخلاف، إلا أن المستخلف غير متعين، فيتشاورون ويتفقون على أحدهم. وإذا خلع الإمام نفسه كان كموته، فينتقل الأمر إلى ولي العهد.

title: Acquisition by force and the duty of obedience
en: The third is coercion and the seizure of power. If the imam dies and someone possessing the qualifications for the imamate puts himself forward without a pledge of allegiance or designation as successor, and subdues the people through his effective power, the caliphate is constituted for him. On the more evident view, the same applies even if he is morally corrupt or ignorant, although he sins by what he has done. A person is not regarded as imam merely because he alone possesses the qualifications for the imamate. The imam must be obeyed so long as he does not contravene a ruling of the revealed Law, whether he is just or unjust. On the more evident view, two imams may not be appointed at the same time. If an imam is established through coercion and predominance, and another subsequently comes and overpowers him, the former is deposed and the conqueror becomes imam.

title: Deposition and the qualification attributed to al-Juwaynī
en: The imam may not be deposed without a reason, and if people depose him without one, their act has no effect. If he removes himself, he is deposed if this is because he is unable to discharge the office; otherwise he is not. He is not deposed by moral corruption or loss of consciousness, but he is deposed by insanity, blindness, deafness, inability to speak, or an illness that causes him to forget his learning. The Imām al-Ḥaramayn says: if the ruler of the time acts unjustly, his oppression and violence become manifest, and verbal admonition does not restrain him from his misconduct, those empowered to bind and loose may agree to restrain him, even by taking up arms and waging war.
ar: ولا يجوز خلع الإمام بلا سبب، ولو خلعوه لم ينفذ. وإن عزل نفسه فإن كان لعجزه عن القيام بالأمر انعزل وإلا فلا. ولا ينعزل الإمام بالفسق والإغماء، وينعزل بالجنون وبالعمى والصمم والخرس وبالمرض الذي ينسيه العلوم. قال إمام الحرمين: وإذا جار والي الوقت فظهر ظلمه وغشمه، ولم يرعو لزاجر عن سوء صنيعه بالقول، فلأهل الحل والعقد التواطؤ على ردعه، ولو بشهر السلاح ونصب الحروب.

If he removes himself, he is deposed if this is because he is unable to discharge the office; otherwise he is not. title: Why the theologians incorporated the subject
en: Nevertheless, corrupt beliefs and disagreements concerning the imamate became widespread among people—indeed, insipid disagreements—especially among the Rāfiḍī and Khārijite sects. Each group inclined towards partisanship that almost led to the abandonment of many principles of Islam, the overturning of Muslim beliefs, and attacks upon the rightly guided caliphs. Although investigation of those caliphs’ circumstances, entitlement to office, and relative merit certainly has little bearing on the actions of persons subject to religious obligation, the theologians attached this chapter to the chapters of kalām. They sometimes even included it in their definition of the discipline, saying that it is the science investigating the fundamental matters concerning the Maker, prophecy, the imamate, the return hereafter, and connected subjects according to the principles of Islam.

title: Definition and exclusions
en: The imamate is general leadership in religious and worldly affairs in succession to the Prophet, blessings and peace be upon him. This last qualification excludes prophecy. The qualification “general” excludes such offices as judgeship and leadership over particular regions. It likewise excludes the authority of someone whom the imam appoints as his unrestricted deputy, since that authority does not extend to the imamate itself.
ar: والإمامة رئاسة عامة في أمر الدين والدنيا خلافة عن النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام. وبهذا القيد خرجت النبوة، وبقيد العموم مثل القضاء والرئاسة في بعض النواحي، وكذا رئاسة من جعله الإمام نائبا عنه على الإطلاق فإنها لا تعم الإمامة.

title: Is unity a condition or a constituent of the definition?
en: Imam al-Rāzī defines it as general leadership in religion and worldly affairs belonging to one individual, and says that this excludes the whole community when it deposes an imam for moral corruption. By “the whole community” he apparently means those empowered to bind and loose, considering their leadership over everyone else or over each individual member of the community. Even so, the objection arises that unity is a condition of the imamate, not a constituent of its essence. There are numerous conditions, and evidence is required to establish them. It may, however, be said that unity more closely resembles an essential constituent: in that situation the whole community is not called “imams”, unlike an ignorant or morally corrupt imam and the like. On this account, two persons to whom the community has pledged allegiance should not both be called imams.
ar: وقال الإمام الرازي: هي رئاسة عامة في الدين والدنيا لشخص واحد من الأشخاص، وقال: هو احتراز عن كل الأمة إذا عزلوا الإمام لفسقه. وكأنه أراد بكل الأمة أهل الحل والعقد واعتبر رياستهم على من عداهم أو على كل من آحاد الأمة. ومع هذا يرد عليه أن الوحدة من شرائط الإمامة لا من مقوماتها، وفي الشروط كثرة وعلى اشتراطها أدلة. ويمكن أن يقال إنها بالمقومات أشبه، من جهة أنه لا يقال لجميع الأمة حينئذ أئمة، بخلاف الإمام الجاهل أو الفاسق أو نحو ذلك. وعلى هذا ينبغي أن لا يقال لشخصين بايعتهما الأمة إنهما إمامان.

title: Succession may be mediated
en: An objection may be raised: succession to the Prophet applies only to someone whom the Prophet appointed as successor. The definition therefore does not apply to an imamate constituted through allegiance or the like—let alone to the leadership of the imam’s general deputy. We reply: even if this is conceded, appointment as successor includes appointment through an intermediary as well as appointment without one. He says: this chapter contains investigations explaining the obligation of the imamate, its conditions, the way it is established, some of its rulings, the identification of the rightful imam after the Prophet, the imamates of the four caliphs, and their ranking in merit.
ar: فإن قيل: الخلافة عن النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام إنما تكون فيمن استخلفه النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام، ولا يصدق التعريف على إمامة البيعة ونحوها، فضلا عن رئاسة النائب العام للإمام. قلنا: لو سلم فالاستخلاف أعم من أن يكون بوسط أو بدونه. قال: وفيه مباحث لبيان وجوب الإمامة وشروطها وطريق ثبوتها ونبذ من أحكامها وتعيين الإمام الحق بعد النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام وإمامة الأئمة الأربعة وترتيبهم في الأفضلية.

title: The competing positions
en: He says: Investigation One, the appointment of an imam. After the age of prophecy has ended, appointing an imam is an obligation upon us established through revelation, according to the Sunnis and the generality of the Muʿtazila; according to al-Jāḥiẓ, al-Khayyāṭ, al-Kaʿbī, and Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī, it is established by reason. The Shiʿa and the Sabʿiyya maintain that it is obligatory upon God. The latter are a group of heretics so called because their predecessors held that the imams number seven: some stopped with the seventh, Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, while others went beyond him, holding that the imams follow cycles of seven, like the days of the week. According to them, the purpose is that the imam should be a teacher in the knowledge of God; according to some Shiʿa, namely the Imāmiyya, it is that he should provide assistance conducive to performing rationally obligatory acts and avoiding rationally reprehensible ones; and according to others, namely the extremists, it is for teaching languages, the properties of foods, medicines and poisons, crafts and trades, and for protection against afflictions and dangers.
ar: قال: المبحث الأول نصب الإمام. بعد انقراض زمن النبوة واجب علينا سمعا عند أهل السنة وعامة المعتزلة، وعقلا عند الجاحظ والخياط والكعبي وأبي الحسين البصري. وقالت الشيعة والسبعية، وهم قوم من الملاحدة سموا بذلك لأن متقدميهم قالوا الأئمة تكون سبعة، وعند السابع وهو محمد بن إسماعيل توقف بعضهم عليه وجاوزه بعضهم وقالوا الأئمة تدور على سبعة سبعة كأيام الأسبوع: هو واجب على الله. فعندهم ليكون معلما في معرفة الله تعالى، وعند بعض الشيعة وهم الإمامية ليكون لطفا في أداء الواجبات العقلية واجتناب المقبحات العقلية، وعند بعضهم وهم الغلاة لتعليم اللغات وأحوال الأغذية والأدوية والسموم والحرف والصناعات والمحافظة عن الآفات والمخافات.

unit_notes: The classifications and the epithet “heretics” reproduce al-Taftāzānī’s polemical account; they are not independently validated descriptions of all the groups named. Luṭf is rendered “assistance conducive to …”: a technical term for what brings an agent closer to obedience and farther from disobedience, not simply kindness. en_html: He says: Investigation One, the appointment of an imam. After the age of prophecy has ended, appointing an imam is an obligation upon us established through revelation, according to the Sunnis and the generality of the Muʿtazila; according to al-Jāḥiẓ, al-Khayyāṭ, al-Kaʿbī, and Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī, it is established by reason. title: Those denying or qualifying the obligation
en: The Najadāt, a Khārijite group following Najda ibn ʿUwaymir, say that it is not obligatory at all. Abū Bakr al-Aṣamm of the Muʿtazila says that it is not obligatory when justice and equity prevail, since it is not needed, but is obligatory when oppression prevails. Hishām al-Fuwaṭī, also of the Muʿtazila, holds the reverse: it is obligatory when justice prevails, to make the ordinances of the Law manifest, but not when oppression prevails, since the oppressors may refuse to obey the imam and he may become a cause of increased disorder.

title: First proof: the Companions’ consensus
en: We have several arguments for its obligatory character. The first, and the principal one, is the consensus of the Companions. They treated this as the most important obligation, attending to it before the burial of the Messenger; they acted similarly after the death of each subsequent imam. It is related that when the Prophet died, Abū Bakr addressed the people: “People! Whoever worshipped Muḥammad, Muḥammad has died. Whoever worshipped Muḥammad’s Lord, He lives and does not die. This affair must have someone to undertake it. Consider the matter and give your opinions—may God have mercy upon you.” They hastened from every side and said: “You have spoken truly; let us consider this affair.” No one said that an imam was unnecessary.
ar: لنا على الوجوب وجوه. الأول وهو العمدة إجماع الصحابة، حتى جعلوا ذلك أهم الواجبات واشتغلوا به عن دفن الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم، وكذا عقيب موت كل إمام. روي أنه لما توفي النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم خطب أبو بكر رضي الله عنه فقال: أيها الناس، من كان يعبد محمدا فإن محمدا قد مات، ومن كان يعبد رب محمد فإنه حي لا يموت. لا بد لهذا الأمر ممن يقوم به، فانظروا وهاتوا آراءكم رحمكم الله. فتبادروا من كل جانب وقالوا: صدقت، ولكن ننظر في هذا الأمر. ولم يقل أحد إنه لا حاجة إلى الإمام.

title: Second proof: a prerequisite of an unconditional obligation
en: The second is that the Lawgiver has commanded the implementation of prescribed punishments, the defence of the frontiers, the preparation of armies for warfare, and numerous matters pertaining to the preservation of order and the protection of the Muslim community, which cannot be accomplished without an imam. Whatever lies within one’s power and is indispensable to an unconditional obligation is itself obligatory, as explained at the beginning of the book. One cannot object: “If the command to implement punishments—for example, amputation in theft—is conditional upon the existence of an imam, it is not unconditional and therefore does not entail an obligation to appoint one, just as the command to pay alms does not entail an obligation to acquire the minimum assessable amount. If it is not conditional upon him, the matter is evident.” We reply that restricting the obligation differs from restricting the act that is obligatory. Here the obligation is unconditional: it has not been restricted or made conditional upon the existence of an imam. The obligatory act—the act commanded—is, however, conditional upon him and depends upon him, just as prayer is obligatory although the prayer itself is conditional upon purification. In the case of alms, by contrast, the obligation itself is conditional upon possession of the minimum assessable amount: when that is absent, there is no obligation.

title: Third proof: the benefits of public authority
en: The third is that appointing an imam brings innumerable benefits and averts manifest harms, and whatever does so is obligatory. The major premise is established by consensus. The minor almost belongs among self-evident truths—indeed, among matters directly witnessed—and may be counted among things seen that require no explanation. Hence the familiar saying that the ruler restrains more than the Qurʾān restrains, and that what is brought into concord by the tongue is not brought into order by demonstration. Social association conducive to well-being in this life and the next cannot be achieved without a coercive authority that repels corruption, preserves interests, and prevents what natural inclinations rush towards and ambitions dispute over. A sufficient witness is the disorder and affliction visibly brought about merely by the death of the person who protects the domain and safeguards the community, even when he lacks the requisite rectitude and soundness and is not wholly free from evil and corruption. Thus even the smallest association, such as a company of travellers, cannot be ordered without a leader whose judgement they follow and whose commands and prohibitions guide them. Something similar may even occur among non-speaking animals: bees have a chief that occupies the position of a leader, through which their affairs remain ordered while it is among them. When it perishes, the individuals scatter like locusts, and destruction and disorder spread among them.
ar: الثالث أن في نصب الإمام استجلاب منافع لا تحصى واستدفاع مضار لا تخفى، وكل ما هو كذلك فهو واجب. أما الكبرى فبالإجماع، وأما الصغرى فيكاد يلحق بالضروريات بل المشاهدات ويعد من العيان الذي لا يحتاج إلى البيان. ولهذا اشتهر أن ما يزع السلطان أكثر مما يزع القرآن، وما يلتئم باللسان لا ينتظم بالبرهان. وذلك لأن الاجتماع المؤدي إلى صلاح المعاش والمعاد لا يتم بدون سلطان قاهر يدرأ المفاسد ويحفظ المصالح ويمنع ما تتسارع إليه الطباع وتتنازع عليه الأطماع. وكفاك شاهدا ما يشاهد من استيلاء الفتن والابتلاء بالمحن لمجرد هلاك من يقوم بحماية الحوزة ورعاية البيضة، وإن لم يكن على ما ينبغي من الصلاح والسداد ولم يخل عن شائبة شر وفساد. ولهذا لا ينتظم أمر أدنى اجتماع كرفقة طريق بدون رئيس يصدرون عن رأيه ومقتضى أمره ونهيه. بل ربما يجري مثل هذا فيما بين الحيوانات العجم كالنحل لها عظيم يقوم مقام الرئيس ينتظم أمرها به ما دام فيها، وإذا هلك انتشرت الأفراد انتشار الجراد وشاع فيما بينها الهلاك والفساد.

title: Why general religious as well as worldly leadership?
en: One cannot object: “At most, this establishes that every association must have an obeyed leader upon whom its order and organisation depend. But how does it follow that his leadership must extend to all people and encompass religious affairs, as is required in an imam?” We reply: ordering the affairs of people generally in a manner conducive to religious and worldly well-being requires general leadership in both. If leaders were multiplied across the regions and territories, this would lead to disputes and conflicts that disrupt order. If his leadership were confined to worldly affairs, religious affairs would lack proper order, although religion is the more important aim and the principal foundation.

en_html: One cannot object: “At most, this establishes that every association must have an obeyed leader upon whom its order and organisation depend. But how does it follow that his leadership must extend to all people and encompass religious affairs, as is required in an imam?” We reply: ordering the affairs of people generally in a manner conducive to religious and worldly well-being requires general leadership in both. If leaders were multiplied across the regions and territories, this would lead to disputes and conflicts that disrupt order. If his leadership were confined to worldly affairs, religious affairs would lack proper order, although religion is the more important aim and the principal foundation.

title: Public benefit does not by itself settle the theory of obligation
en: As for the major premise, according to us it is established by consensus, whereas those who affirm rational obligation regard it as self-evident. The author of the Abridgement of the Muḥaṣṣal objects that the minor premise is demonstrated rationally and concerns goodness and badness, which is not your doctrine, while the major premise is clearer than the minor and therefore requires no appeal to consensus. This is answered by noting that a thing’s being beneficial or harmful does not belong to the disputed question of goodness and badness. Nor is it evident—let alone more evident—that averting harm is obligatory in the sense that someone who omits it deserves punishment from God. Such a point ought not to escape him, nor should a learned scholar be so excessively enamoured of raising objections.
ar: وأما الكبرى فبالإجماع عندنا وبالضرورة عند القائلين بالوجوب العقلي. واعتراض صاحب تلخيص المحصل بأن بيان الصغرى عقلي من باب القبح والحسن وليس من مذهبكم، والكبرى أوضح من الصغرى فلا حاجة إلى التعرض للإجماع، مدفوع بأن كون الشيء صلاحا أو فسادا ليس في شيء من متنازع الحسن والقبح، وكون دفع الضرر واجبا بمعنى استحقاق تاركه العقاب عند الله تعالى ليس بواضح فضلا عن الأوضح. ولا ينبغي أن يخفى مثل هذا عليه ولا أن يكون الرجل العالم العلمي في هذه الغاية من الشغف بالاعتراض.

title: Objection from the harms of political office
en: One cannot object: “Consensus establishes obligation only where the measure does not involve a harm equal to or greater than the harm averted. Here, appointing an imam involves corruptions beyond reckoning: opinions reflect divergent desires, and human dispositions resent being subjected to their equals. People rarely persist in right guidance and conduct worthy of imitation. Souls consequently incline towards refusal and resistance; corruption appears, injustice and obstinacy multiply, crops and offspring are destroyed, and both root and branch disappear. A sufficient witness is what one hears of events from the end of ʿUthmān’s caliphate to the beginning of the Abbasid state.” We reply: compared with its benefits, its harms—and compared with its advantages, its corruptions—are so few that their apparent abundance is disregarded and they are reckoned as nothing.
ar: لا يقال: الإجماع على الوجوب إنما هو إذا لم يتضمن مضرة مثل المضرة المندفعة أو فوقها، وههنا نصب الإمام يتضمن مفاسد لا يضبطها العد والإحصاء لما في الآراء من اختلافات الأهواء وفي الطباع من الاستنكاف عن تسلط الأكفاء. والإنسان قليل البقاء على ما عليه من الاهتداء وصلاح الاقتداء، فتميل النفوس إلى الإباء والاستعصاء ويظهر الفساد ويكثر البغي والعناد ويهلك الحرث والنسل ويذهب الفرع والأصل. وكفاك شاهدا ما تسمع من قصص انقضاء خلافة عثمان رضي الله تعالى عنه إلى ابتداء دولة بني العباس. لأنا نقول: مضاره بالنسبة إلى منافعه ومفاسده بالإضافة إلى مصالحه مما لا يعبأ بكثرته ويلحق بالعدم في قلته.

title: The absence of a fully qualified imam
en: An objection may be raised: “If appointing an imam were obligatory, it would follow that in most ages the community unanimously abandoned an obligation, because there was no imam possessing the requisite qualifications—especially after the end of the Abbasid state. Moreover, the Prophet said: ‘The caliphate after me will last thirty years, then it will become a biting kingship.’ Those years were completed with ʿAlī’s caliphate. Muʿāwiya and his successors were therefore kings and rulers, not imams or caliphs. Yet that consequence is inadmissible: abandoning an obligation is sin and error, and the community does not agree upon error.” We reply: error would follow only if they abandoned it while possessing ability and choice, not through inability and necessity. Furthermore, besides being an individually transmitted report, the hadith admits of being understood as referring to the caliphate in its complete form.
ar: فإن قيل: لو وجب نصب الإمام لزم إطباق الأمة في أكثر الأعصار على ترك الواجب لانتفاء الإمام المتصف بما يجب من الصفات، سيما بعد انقضاء الدولة العباسية، ولقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم: الخلافة بعدي ثلاثون سنة ثم تصير ملكا عضوضا. وقد تم ذلك بخلافة علي رضي الله تعالى عنه، فمعاوية ومن بعده ملوك وأمراء لا أئمة ولا خلفاء. واللازم منتف، لأن ترك الواجب معصية وضلالة والأمة لا تجتمع على الضلالة. قلنا: إنما يلزم الضلالة لو تركوه عن قدرة واختيار لا عجز واضطرار. والحديث مع أنه من باب الآحاد يحتمل الصرف إلى الخلافة على وجه الكمال.

title: A nominal imam without effective power
en: Another question arises here. Suppose no imam possessing the required qualifications exists, and a group of those empowered to bind and loose pledge allegiance to a Qurashī who possesses some of them, but whose rulings are not effective, whose commands are not obeyed by the public, and who lacks the power to manage people’s interests and appoint or dismiss whom he wishes. Does this constitute performance of the obligation? Must the immensely powerful rulers of the outlying regions, who possess sound government, justice, and equity, hand all authority over to him and stand before him like ordinary subjects?
ar: وههنا بحث آخر، وهو أنه إذا لم يوجد إمام على شرائطه وبايع طائفة من أهل الحل والعقد قرشيا فيه بعض الشرائط من غير نفاذ لأحكامه وطاعة من العامة لأوامره وشوكة بها يتصرف في مصالح العباد ويقتدر على النصب والعزل لمن أراد، هل يكون ذلك إتيانا بالواجب؟ وهل يجب على ذوي الشوكة العظيمة من ملوك الأطراف المتصفين بحسن السياسة والعدل والإنصاف أن يفوضوا الأمر إليه بالكلية ويكونوا لديه كسائر الرعية؟

title: A further appeal to revealed commands
en: An argument may also be based on such texts as God’s words, “Obey God, obey the Messenger, and those vested with authority among you,” and the Prophet’s saying, “Whoever dies without knowing the imam of his time dies a death of the age of ignorance.” The obligation to obey and to recognise him requires that he exist. As for why this is not an obligation upon us established by reason, and not an obligation upon God at all, that follows from the earlier refutation of the two underlying principles.
ar: وقد يتمسك بمثل قوله تعالى: أطيعوا الله وأطيعوا الرسول وأولي الأمر منكم، وقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم: من مات ولم يعرف إمام زمانه مات ميتة جاهلية. فإن وجوب الطاعة والمعرفة يقتضي وجوب الحصول. وأما أنه لا يجب علينا عقلا ولا على الله أصلا فلما مر من بطلان الأصلين.

en_html: An argument may also be based on such texts as God’s words, “Obey God, obey the Messenger, and those vested with authority among you,” and the Prophet’s saying, “Whoever dies without knowing the imam of his time dies a death of the age of ignorance.” The obligation to obey and to recognise him requires that he exist. As for why this is not an obligation upon us established by reason, and not an obligation upon God at all, that follows from the earlier refutation of the two underlying principles.
